cadence: daily, 7 days a week, noon America/New_York

days.title: Who's who: the machinery of the securities industry
understand: Issuer -> underwriter -> investor (primary) vs investor -> BD -> investor (secondary): where the cash goes in each
Broker (agent, earns commission, no inventory risk) vs dealer (principal, earns markup/markdown, carries inventory)
Life of a trade end to end: order -> execution venue -> trade report -> clearing (NSCC) -> settlement (DTC) -> custody -> transfer agent/registrar records
Why market makers exist: immediacy for a price (the spread) and the inventory risk they carry
First/second/third/fourth markets as a map of venue x intermediary
The regulator cast list: SEC above SROs (FINRA, MSRB, exchanges); Fed for credit; Treasury/FinCEN/OFAC; SIPC vs FDIC; states and NASAA
The eight laws in one sentence each, and which market (primary vs secondary) each governs
memorize: broker vs dealer
first/second/third/fourth markets
law -> year -> what it does
SIPC vs FDIC limits
MSRB writes rules but does not enforce
FINRA formed 2007 (NASD + NYSE member regulation)
traps: A firm cannot act as broker and dealer in the same trade
Third market = listed security traded OTC; fourth = institution-to-institution with no BD (ATS/ECN)
SIPC is not insurance against market loss and does not cover commodities/futures
The '33 Act did not create the SEC; the '34 Act did
Custodian vs transfer agent vs registrar vs clearing firm — four different jobs
calculations: Markup % = (price to customer - prevailing market price) / prevailing market price
Commission vs markup: which appears on the confirmation and why
trader_connection: Market makers -> liquidity, spreads and inventory risk; your P&L as a dealer is spread capture minus adverse selection minus inventory drift
Clearing -> counterparty risk reduction: novation to NSCC/OCC turns thousands of bilateral exposures into one netted exposure to a CCP
Custody chain -> where your securities actually sit when you lend or pledge them (DTC -> custodian -> BD -> you in street name)
also_cover: Order flow terms from the sample exam: broker earns a commission (agent); dealer earns a markup (principal); OTC = not on an exchange
Second market = unlisted stocks OTC (use this SIE definition)

days.title: Economics, the Fed and how macro moves prices
understand: Business cycle phases (expansion, peak, contraction, trough) and what each does to earnings, credit spreads and rates
GDP (nominal vs real), CPI and inflation vs disinflation vs deflation — level vs rate of change
Leading, coincident and lagging indicators — why each is classified where it is
Monetary policy (Fed: money supply and rates) vs fiscal policy (Congress/President: taxes and spending)
Fed tools: open-market operations, discount rate, reserve requirements (0% since 2020), interest on reserve balances
Yield curve shapes (normal, inverted, flat) and why inversion is read as a recession signal
Currency effects: stronger dollar -> cheaper imports, weaker US exporters, lower dollar value of foreign earnings
memorize: leading/coincident/lagging indicator lists
Fed tools and which is used most
FOMC meets 8 times a year
recession exam convention (two consecutive quarters of declining real GDP; NBER makes the official call)
fed funds rate vs discount rate vs prime rate vs broker call rate
traps: Fiscal policy is NOT the Fed
Buying securities in OMO is easing (adds reserves); selling is tightening
Stock prices are a leading indicator; CPI and duration of unemployment lag
An inverted curve means short rates above long rates
Deflation (falling prices) vs disinflation (slowing inflation)
calculations: Real rate ~= nominal rate - inflation
Chain: Fed hikes -> short yields up -> existing bond prices down -> borrowing costs up -> equity multiples compress -> dollar tends to firm
trader_connection: Fed policy -> rates/FX/equity/commodity transmission; the 2s10s spread as a positioning signal
Rates desks hedge with Treasury futures and SOFR futures because the curve moves on Fed expectations, not just the level
also_cover: Market structures: monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition, perfect competition (with examples)
Fed tools as the SIE lists them: open-market operations, discount rate, reserve requirements, and Regulation T (exam convention)
Rates and inflation: the Fed raises rates to fight inflation; know the causal lever the exam wants

days.title: Common stock: ownership, votes and corporate actions
understand: What a share is: residual claim, limited liability, last in liquidation
Authorized, issued, outstanding and treasury stock — and why buybacks change EPS
Statutory vs cumulative voting and why cumulative favors minority holders
Proxies and why they exist
Preemptive rights and anti-dilution
Dividend mechanics: declaration, ex-date, record date, payable date — and why under T+1 the ex-date equals the record date
Cash dividends vs stock dividends vs forward/reverse splits: what changes and what does not (total value)
How exchange price adjusts on the ex-date
memorize: declaration -> ex -> record -> payable sequence
ex-date = record date under T+1 (since May 28, 2024)
mutual fund ex-date set by the fund (usually the business day after record date)
cumulative voting formula
traps: Buy on the ex-date and you do NOT get the dividend
Treasury stock has no vote and no dividend
Stock dividends and splits do not change the holder's total value or cost basis in total
Voting rights belong to common, generally not preferred
Record date vs ex-date vs payable date
calculations: Cumulative voting: votes = shares x seats up for election
Split math: new shares = old x (new/old); new price = old x (old/new)
Stock dividend: 10% stock dividend -> 1.1x shares, price / 1.1
Dividend yield = annual dividend / price
trader_connection: Corporate actions -> index rebalancing and options contract adjustments (OCC adjusts strikes and deliverables for splits)
Dividend dates drive early-exercise decisions on calls and dividend-arbitrage/dividend-capture in stock loan
also_cover: Cash-settlement ex-date = the business day AFTER the record date; regular-way ex-date = record date
Tax event for a cash dividend = the payable date
Split math with share counts and price; who approves splits (state law/charter, not a FINRA rule)

days.title: Preferred stock, rights, warrants and ADRs
understand: Preferred as a hybrid: fixed dividend, priority over common, usually no vote — why its price behaves like a bond
Cumulative, participating, convertible, callable, adjustable-rate preferred — what each feature is worth and to whom
Rights: short-term, issued to existing holders at a discount (preemptive), trade separately
Warrants: long-term, issued with bonds/preferred as a sweetener, strike above market at issue
ADRs: foreign shares held by a US depositary bank; dollar-denominated; currency risk remains; sponsored vs unsponsored
memorize: rights vs warrants (term, price vs market, who gets them)
cumulative preferred arrears must be paid before common dividends
ADR holders face currency risk and foreign withholding
preferred dividends are not a legal obligation (vs bond interest)
traps: Rights = discount + short term; warrants = premium + long term
Callable preferred pays a higher dividend to compensate for call risk
Convertible preferred pays a LOWER dividend (the conversion option is worth something)
ADRs trade in dollars but the underlying currency still moves the price
calculations: Preferred price ~ annual dividend / required yield (interest-rate sensitivity)
Cumulative arrears = missed dividends x shares
Conversion ratio = par / conversion price; parity price = common price x conversion ratio
trader_connection: Preferred = rate + credit exposure in equity clothing; hedgers treat it as long-duration credit
Warrants and convertibles = embedded long call options -> delta, vega and dilution
also_cover: Preferred par is typically $100; preferred suits income investors, not capital appreciation
Rights: one right per share, short life, intrinsic value at issue; warrants: long life, no intrinsic value at issue

days.title: Bond math: price, yield and why they move opposite
understand: Par, coupon (nominal yield), maturity, price as % of par
Why price and yield move inversely — the fixed coupon is repriced to the market yield
Current yield, YTM, YTC — what each measures and what each ignores
Premium bond: Coupon > Current Yield > YTM > YTC — because the premium is lost faster if called early
Discount bond: YTC > YTM > Current Yield > Coupon — because the discount is gained faster if called early
Duration intuition: longer maturity and lower coupon -> more price sensitivity; zeros have duration = maturity
Quote conventions: points, 1/8s, 32nds, basis points
Accrued interest: who pays whom and why
memorize: 1 bond point = $10; 1/8 point = $1.25; 1 bp = 0.01%
Treasury 32nds: 1/32 = $0.3125 per $1,000
corporate & muni accrue 30/360; government actual/actual
accrued interest runs from last coupon date up to but not including settlement date
premium and discount yield orderings
traps: 'Nominal yield' is the coupon
Current yield uses PRICE, not par
A premium bond's YTM is BELOW its coupon
Buyer pays seller accrued interest
Rates up -> long-maturity, low-coupon bonds fall most
calculations: Current yield = annual coupon $ / market price
Accrued interest = principal x coupon x days/360 (30/360 month counting)
Yield relationship ordering proofs with numbers
Approximate YTM = (coupon + (par - price)/years) / ((par + price)/2)
trader_connection: Bonds -> duration/rate hedging: DV01, why a desk sells Treasury futures to hedge a long corporate book
Negative convexity of callable bonds — the same shape as being short a call
also_cover: Quote conversion drills: corporate 86 5/8 = $866.25; Treasury 106-16 = $1,065.00 (buy at the ask)
Yield ordering questions phrased 'lowest to highest' as well as 'highest to lowest'

days.title: Corporate debt: seniority, collateral, calls and conversions
understand: Secured (mortgage, equipment trust, collateral trust) vs unsecured (debentures, subordinated debentures)
Liquidation priority: secured -> unsecured/general creditors -> subordinated -> preferred -> common
Indenture, trustee and the Trust Indenture Act of 1939
Call and put features, call protection, refunding, sinking funds
Convertible bonds: conversion ratio, parity, why issuers pay a lower coupon
Zero-coupon bonds: OID, phantom income (annual accretion taxed for corporate zeros)
Credit ratings: investment grade (BBB-/Baa3 and above) vs high-yield; what spreads compensate for
memorize: liquidation priority order
investment grade = BBB-/Baa3 and above
equipment trust certificates -> transportation (airlines, railroads)
collateral trust -> backed by securities held in trust
Trust Indenture Act -> corporate bonds, trustee protects bondholders
traps: Debentures are unsecured — backed by full faith and credit of the issuer
Income (adjustment) bonds pay only if earned — used in reorganizations
Zeros have no reinvestment risk but maximum interest-rate risk
Munis and Treasuries are exempt from the Trust Indenture Act
Call risk rises when rates FALL
calculations: Conversion ratio = par / conversion price
Parity: bond price / ratio = parity stock price
Zero accretion: annual OID = (par - purchase price) / years (straight-line teaching convention)
trader_connection: Capital structure -> credit hedging with CDS and recovery assumptions; seniority sets recovery
Convertibles -> equity delta + credit + vol; convert arb is long bond, short stock
also_cover: Call protection = years until the FIRST call date; call premium = call price minus par (e.g., 105 -> $50)
Mortgage bonds are backed by real property the corporation owns

days.title: Governments, agencies, mortgage-backed and money-market paper
understand: T-bills (discount), notes, bonds, TIPS (principal indexed to CPI), STRIPS (zeros)
Treasury auctions: competitive vs non-competitive bids; the single-price (Dutch) auction
Agencies: GNMA (explicit full faith and credit, fully taxable) vs FNMA/FHLMC (GSEs, implied backing)
Pass-throughs and CMOs: prepayment risk (rates fall) vs extension risk (rates rise); PAC, TAC, companion and Z tranches
Money market instruments: commercial paper (max 270 days to be exempt), bankers' acceptances, negotiable CDs, repos, fed funds, T-bills
Why money-market instruments are short, liquid and low-risk — and what 'breaking the buck' meant
memorize: T-bill maturities (4, 6, 8, 13, 17, 26, 52 weeks)
notes 2-10 years, bonds 20-30 years
Treasury interest: federal taxable, state exempt
GNMA = only agency with explicit US guarantee
commercial paper exempt from registration if <= 270 days
BAs finance international trade
traps: T-bills are quoted on a discount-yield basis — bid yield higher than ask yield
GNMA interest is taxable at all levels
CMOs have prepayment AND extension risk; PACs have the most protection, companions the least
Repo is a collateralized loan, not a sale for economic purposes
TIPS: inflation adjusts PRINCIPAL; the coupon rate is fixed
calculations: T-bill discount yield vs bond-equivalent yield intuition
TIPS: new principal = principal x (1 + CPI change); coupon $ = rate x adjusted principal
trader_connection: Repo -> the financing engine of every rates desk; haircuts = collateral margin
MBS -> negative convexity; mortgage servicers and MBS holders hedge by buying duration when rates fall
Treasury basis trade: cash Treasury vs futures, financed in repo
also_cover: Commercial paper and banker's acceptances: max 270 days; CP typically sold in $100,000+ denominations to institutions
Treasury bills are money-market instruments; unsecured, backed by full faith and credit

days.title: Municipal securities: tax-exempt credit
understand: GO bonds (taxing power, voter approval, debt limits) vs revenue bonds (project revenue, feasibility study, covenants)
Double-barreled, moral obligation, special tax, special assessment, IDRs (corporate credit!)
Short-term notes: TAN, RAN, TRAN, BAN, GAN, CLN — what cash flow backs each
Tax treatment: federal exemption, in-state exemption, territories triple-exempt, capital gains taxable
Tax-equivalent yield and who munis suit (high brackets, not IRAs)
MSRB: rules only; enforcement by FINRA (BDs), SEC, bank regulators (banks); EMMA; G-37 political contributions
Official statement vs prospectus; municipal advisors
memorize: TEY = muni yield / (1 - tax rate)
muni yield equivalent = taxable yield x (1 - tax rate)
MSRB created by Securities Acts Amendments of 1975
G-37 de minimis $250 per election (only where the MFP can vote); 2-year ban
muni trades reported to RTRS within 15 minutes
MIG ratings for short-term muni notes
traps: IDRs are backed by a CORPORATION's lease payments, not the municipality
Munis in an IRA waste the tax exemption
Munis are exempt from '33 Act registration but NOT from antifraud rules
MSRB does not enforce its own rules
Capital gains on munis are taxable
calculations: TEY and after-tax yield comparisons
Muni premium amortization (basis steps down; no deductible loss at maturity)
trader_connection: Munis -> credit and tax-adjusted yield; the muni/Treasury ratio as a relative-value signal
Muni desks hedge rate risk with Treasury futures but carry basis risk because munis do not move 1:1
also_cover: Muni quotes: serial bonds (often GO) quoted on a yield basis; term 'dollar bonds' (often revenue) quoted as % of par
Municipal Finance Professional: RR who solicits municipal ISSUER business; an RR who only sells munis to retail is not an MFP
Convention-center bonds = revenue bonds = exempt securities

days.title: Risk: every way an investment can hurt you
understand: Systematic (market, interest-rate, inflation/purchasing-power, currency, political) vs unsystematic (business, credit, regulatory for one firm) — diversification only kills the second

Each of the 18 risks with one concrete market example: market, systematic, unsystematic, credit, default, liquidity, interest-rate, reinvestment, inflation, political, legislative, regulatory, currency, business, call, prepayment, counterparty, leverage
Beta as a measure of systematic risk; standard deviation as total volatility
Which products carry which risks — the product/risk matrix the SIE loves
memorize: systematic vs unsystematic list
reinvestment risk: highest for high-coupon callable bonds; none for zeros
purchasing-power risk: highest for fixed-income and cash
liquidity/marketability risk examples (DPPs, non-traded REITs)
traps: Diversification does NOT reduce systematic risk
Legislative risk = law changes (e.g., tax law); regulatory = regulator rule changes
Call risk and prepayment risk are the same shape: you get your money back when rates fall
Credit risk (downgrade) vs default risk (failure to pay)
Liquidity risk vs marketability
calculations: Beta interpretation: beta 1.5 -> ~1.5x market moves
Leverage: 2:1 leverage doubles percentage gains and losses
trader_connection: Risk taxonomy -> the risk manager's factor map: rates, credit, equity, FX, vol, liquidity, counterparty
Counterparty risk -> why OTC derivatives are collateralized under CSAs and why clearing exists
Leverage risk -> margin calls turn price risk into liquidity risk (the 2021 Archegos pattern)
also_cover: Regulatory risk (agency rules) vs legislative risk (new laws) vs business risk vs market risk, with scenarios

days.title: Options I: the contract, the premium and who owes what
understand: A call is the right to BUY; a put is the right to SELL; the buyer (holder) has rights, the writer (seller) has obligations
Premium = intrinsic value + time value; intrinsic can never be negative
ITM/ATM/OTM for calls vs puts
Exercise vs assignment; OCC as issuer/guarantor and random/FIFO assignment by BDs
Standardized terms: 100 shares, expiration, American vs European, strike intervals
Account opening for options: ODD delivery at or before approval, ROP approval, signed agreement within 15 days of approval
Settlement: equity options T+1; exercise settles T+1 in stock; index options cash-settled
memorize: contract = 100 shares
ODD delivered no later than account approval
options agreement returned within 15 days after approval
American = exercise any time; European = only at expiration
index options settle in cash
long options (<= 9 months) must be paid in full
traps: Bullish positions: BUY CALL, SELL PUT; bearish: BUY PUT, SELL CALL
Time value decays toward zero at expiration
An OTM option has NO intrinsic value — all premium is time value
The writer, not the buyer, can be assigned
Call ITM when market > strike; put ITM when market < strike
calculations: Intrinsic: call = max(0, S - K); put = max(0, K - S)
Time value = premium - intrinsic
Contract $ = premium x 100
trader_connection: Options -> nonlinear exposure; delta, gamma and theta as the sensitivities behind 'time value'
Assignment risk around dividends — short calls get assigned the day before ex-date
also_cover: Standard equity options: expire on the third Friday of the month; last trade 4:00 p.m. ET; expiration 11:59 p.m. ET — watch time-zone conversions in answer choices
Calls gain intrinsic value as the market rises; puts as it falls

days.title: Options II: four positions, hedges and spreads
understand: BUY CALL: bullish, max loss premium, max gain unlimited, BE = strike + premium
SELL CALL (naked): bearish/neutral, max gain premium, max loss unlimited, BE = strike + premium
BUY PUT: bearish, max loss premium, max gain strike - premium, BE = strike - premium
SELL PUT: bullish/neutral, max gain premium, max loss strike - premium, BE = strike - premium
Covered call: income, caps upside; protective put: insurance on long stock; BUY CALL to protect a short stock position
Spreads: debit vs credit, bull vs bear, how to tell which from the strikes
Straddles (long = expect volatility, short = expect calm)
Hedging logic as exposure transformation
memorize: breakeven formulas for all four positions
calls up (BE = strike + premium), puts down (BE = strike - premium)
covered call BE = stock cost - premium
protective put BE = stock cost + premium
traps: Selling a naked call has UNLIMITED risk; selling a put's risk is limited to strike - premium
Covered call does not protect against a large decline
Debit spread: you want it to WIDEN; credit spread: you want it to EXPIRE
Buyers want volatility; sellers want time decay
Protecting a SHORT stock position = BUY CALL (not buy put)
calculations: Max gain/loss/BE for each position and for covered/protective combos
Spread max gain/loss and BE
Straddle BEs = strike +/- total premium
trader_connection: Options -> nonlinear hedging: a protective put is a floor, a covered call a sold cap; collars finance one with the other
Derivatives -> exposure transformation: the same payoff built from stock + options (put-call parity intuition)
also_cover: Short stock + long call combined max gain/loss (e.g., short 100 at 52, long 55 call at 3: max gain $4,900, max loss $600)

days.title: Mutual funds: NAV, loads and share classes
understand: Investment Company Act of 1940: face-amount, UIT, management companies (open-end vs closed-end); diversified 75-5-10
NAV vs POP; forward pricing; redemption within 7 days
Sales charges: max 8.5% of POP; Class A (front load, breakpoints), B (CDSC, converts to A), C (level load, 12b-1), no-load
12b-1 fees: max 1%; 'no-load' only if 12b-1 <= 0.25%
Breakpoints, rights of accumulation, letters of intent (13 months, backdate 90 days); breakpoint selling is prohibited
Fund roles: board of directors, investment adviser, custodian, transfer agent, principal underwriter/sponsor
Dividend and capital-gain distributions and their taxation even when reinvested
memorize: max sales charge 8.5% of POP
12b-1 max 1% (0.75% distribution + 0.25% service)
LOI 13 months, 90-day backdating
redemption within 7 calendar days
at least 40% independent directors
75-5-10 diversification
traps: Sales charge % is a percent of POP, not NAV
Class A is usually best for large, long-term investors; C for short horizons
Reinvested distributions are still taxable
The custodian holds assets; the transfer agent handles shareholder records and distributions
Breakpoints reduce Class A front-end loads; C shares have no front load, so breakpoints do not help a C-share buyer
calculations: Sales charge % = (POP - NAV) / POP
POP = NAV / (1 - sales charge %)
Shares purchased = dollars / POP
trader_connection: Fund plumbing -> daily NAV strike, creations/redemptions and liquidity mismatch risk
Fund cash flows as market flows: outflows force selling
also_cover: Fund types by objective: growth, income, growth & income (stocks), balanced (stocks + bonds), sector, index, bond, money market
Class B shares: CDSC declines over time, suit smaller purchases held longer; custodian holds fund assets

days.title: Exchange-traded, closed-end, UITs and the alternatives
understand: Closed-end funds: fixed shares, exchange-traded, premium/discount to NAV
ETFs: creation/redemption by authorized participants and the arbitrage that keeps price near NAV; ETNs as unsecured debt
Leveraged and inverse ETFs: daily reset and path dependence (FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-31)
UITs: fixed portfolio, no board, no active management, redeemable units
REITs: 75% real-estate assets/income tests, 90% distribution, equity vs mortgage vs hybrid, traded vs non-traded
DPPs/limited partnerships: pass-through income and losses, GP vs LP roles, passive-loss rules, illiquidity
Hedge funds and private funds: accredited/qualified investors, lockups, leverage, limited liquidity
memorize: REIT must distribute >= 90% of taxable income
REIT dividends are generally ordinary income
LP liability limited to investment; GP unlimited
passive losses offset only passive income
ETN = issuer credit risk
traps: Closed-end funds are NOT redeemed by the fund — you sell on the exchange
REITs pass through income but NOT losses; DPPs pass through both
Leveraged ETFs are generally unsuitable for buy-and-hold
UITs do not have an investment adviser actively managing
Non-traded REITs carry high liquidity risk
calculations: Premium/discount = (price - NAV) / NAV
Leveraged ETF decay example over two volatile days
trader_connection: ETF creation/redemption -> AP arbitrage is a basis trade; ETF liquidity layers (screen vs underlying)
Leveraged ETFs rebalance at the close — their hedging flows move markets late in the day
also_cover: Real estate programs: depreciation, deductible interest, pass-through losses; depletion belongs to oil & gas programs
Hybrid REITs hold properties and mortgages

days.title: Annuities and insurance-linked products
understand: Fixed annuities (insurer's general account, not a security) vs variable annuities (separate account, a security; registered)
Accumulation units vs annuity units; assumed interest rate (AIR)
Settlement options: life only, life with period certain, joint and last survivor, unit refund
Indexed annuities; variable life overview
Taxation: after-tax contributions, earnings taxed as ordinary income, LIFO on withdrawals, 10% penalty before 59 1/2
1035 exchanges; surrender charges; suitability concerns
memorize: VA sub-account returns > AIR -> payment rises; < AIR -> payment falls
life only pays the most per month and stops at death
nonqualified annuity withdrawals: earnings first (LIFO), ordinary income
1035 exchange = tax-free annuity-to-annuity / life-to-annuity
traps: Fixed annuities are NOT securities; variable annuities ARE
Annuity gains are never capital gains
Putting a VA inside an IRA adds cost with no extra tax deferral
AIR is not a guarantee
Life only has the highest payout and the most risk to heirs
calculations: Exclusion ratio intuition for annuitized payments
trader_connection: Annuity writers hedge embedded guarantees with equity options and rate swaps — the dynamic hedging behind variable annuity books
also_cover: Life with period certain: lifetime payments with a guaranteed minimum period to a beneficiary
Immediate annuities need a single (lump-sum) premium; periodic purchase payments mean a deferred annuity

days.title: How securities are born: underwriting and registration
understand: Securities Act of 1933: registration and disclosure; S-1; SEC review does not approve
The IPO timeline: pre-filing -> filing -> cooling-off (min 20 days) -> effective date -> aftermarket
Red herring, IOIs (non-binding), due diligence meeting, blue-sky, final prospectus, prospectus delivery windows
Firm commitment (principal, risk on underwriter) vs best efforts, all-or-none, mini-max (agency)
Syndicate, selling group, spread components (manager's fee, underwriting fee, selling concession)
Tombstone ads, free-writing prospectus, stabilization (at or below POP), Reg M, quiet periods
Follow-ons, shelf registration, primary vs secondary shares
memorize: cooling-off at least 20 days
prospectus delivery: IPO 25 days (listed) / 90 days (unlisted); follow-on 0 (listed) / 40 (unlisted)
stabilizing bid at or below the POP
SEC 'neither approves nor disapproves' disclaimer
selling concession is the largest part of the spread
traps: No sales and no binding commitments during cooling-off — only IOIs
Firm commitment = principal; best efforts = agency
Tombstones are allowed during cooling-off
Selling group members are NOT at risk for unsold shares
Registration effectiveness is not SEC approval
calculations: Spread = POP - price paid to issuer; split into manager fee + underwriting fee + selling concession
Proceeds to issuer = shares x (POP - spread)
trader_connection: Firm commitment -> inventory risk on the underwriter's balance sheet; greenshoe as a stabilization hedge
IPO allocation and stabilization -> short-covering flows in the aftermarket
also_cover: IPO restricted persons (FINRA Rule 5130): member firms, their employees and immediate family (spouse, parents, in-laws, siblings, children, anyone materially supported); grandparents and cousins are NOT restricted

days.title: The exemptions: private placements, Rule 144 and tender offers
understand: Exempt SECURITIES (never register) vs exempt TRANSACTIONS (this deal need not register)
Reg D 506(b) vs 506(c); accredited investor definition; Form D within 15 days
Rule 144: restricted vs control stock, holding periods, affiliate volume limits, Form 144
Rule 144A (QIBs) and Reg S (offshore)
Reg A Tier 1 vs Tier 2; Rule 147/147A intrastate; Reg CF
Tender offers: minimum open period, net-long rule
Beneficial ownership (13D/13G) and Section 16 insiders, short-swing profits
memorize: accredited: $200k/$300k income or $1M net worth ex-residence; Series 7/65/82 holders
506(b): up to 35 non-accredited; no general solicitation
Rule 144 holding: 6 months (reporting issuer) / 1 year (non-reporting)
144 volume: greater of 1% of outstanding or 4-week average weekly volume per 90 days
Form 144 if > 5,000 shares or > $50,000 in 90 days
144A QIB: $100 million
Reg A: Tier 1 $20M, Tier 2 $75M per 12 months
Reg CF: $5M per 12 months
tender offer open >= 20 business days
13D within 5 business days of crossing 5% (amended 2024)
Form 4 within 2 business days; short-swing = 6 months
traps: Commercial paper is exempt only if <= 270 days
Reg D is a transaction exemption — resale is restricted
Control stock can be registered stock held by an affiliate
Rule 147 = intrastate (state registration, not SEC)
Bank STOCK is exempt; bank HOLDING COMPANY stock is not
calculations: Rule 144 volume calculation with numbers
trader_connection: Restricted stock -> hedging concentrated positions (collars, prepaid variable forwards) under 144 constraints
Tender offers and merger arb: why net-long rules exist
also_cover: Offering memorandum (private placement memorandum) -> Reg D; official statement -> munis; prospectus -> registered offering
Tender offers as the takeover route; 5% disclosure (13D) makes a secret stake impossible

days.title: Orders, quotes and the people who make markets
understand: Bid, ask, spread, size; firm vs subject vs nominal quotes; market makers vs specialists/DMMs
Market orders (execution guarantee) vs limit orders (price guarantee) vs stop (trigger to market) vs stop-limit (trigger to limit)
Where stops and limits sit relative to the market (buy limit below, buy stop above; sell limit above, sell stop below)
Time in force: day, GTC, FOK, IOC, AON; not-held orders
Best execution, Reg NMS order protection, ATSs/dark pools, trade reporting
Order tickets: required fields, marking long/short, solicited vs unsolicited, discretionary
memorize: market = execution guarantee; limit = price guarantee
buy stop above market; sell stop below
order ticket must be marked long or short
unsolicited orders marked 'unsolicited'
FOK: all immediately or cancel; IOC: fill what you can, cancel rest; AON: all or nothing but not immediate
traps: A stop order becomes a MARKET order once triggered — no price guarantee
A buy limit order is placed BELOW the market
Stop-limit can be triggered and never fill
A sell stop protects a LONG position (placed below the market); a buy stop protects a SHORT position (placed above)
Bid = where a dealer buys from you; ask = where a dealer sells to you
calculations: Spread = ask - bid
Which trades trigger a stop order (sequence problems)
trader_connection: Market makers -> liquidity, spreads and inventory risk; adverse selection vs spread capture
Stop orders cluster -> stop cascades in fast markets; this is why desks work orders algorithmically
also_cover: Order ticket contents: account, security, buy/sell (sells marked long/short), quantity, order type and limit/stop price, time in force, solicited/unsolicited, discretion; the commission appears on the confirmation, not the ticket
Limit orders guarantee price or better; stop orders guarantee nothing once elected

days.title: Clearing, settlement and custody: what happens after the trade
understand: Regular-way T+1 (since May 28, 2024) for stocks, corporate and muni bonds, government securities and options; cash settlement same day
NSCC netting (CNS), DTC custody/book-entry, DVP/RVP institutional settlement
Street name vs registered name; transfer agent and registrar
Confirmations: at or before completion of the transaction; what they disclose (capacity, markup/commission)
Account statements: at least quarterly
Fails to deliver, buy-ins, good delivery, when-issued trades
Corporate-action processing through DTC and why ex-dates move with settlement cycles
memorize: regular way T+1 for equities, corporates, munis, options and governments
cash settlement = same day
confirmation at or before completion
statements at least quarterly
Reg T payment period = settlement + 2 business days
traps: Settlement date is not trade date
Options exercise settles T+1 in stock
A confirmation is not a statement
DVP means the institution pays only against delivery
When-issued trades settle when the security is issued
calculations: Counting business days to settlement around a holiday
Ex-date given a record date under T+1
trader_connection: Settlement -> counterparty/operational risk; fails cost money (buy-ins, penalties) and funding
T+1 compressed the stock-loan recall window and FX funding for foreign buyers

days.title: Short selling and securities lending
understand: The short as a loan: borrow -> sell -> post collateral -> buy to cover -> return shares
Reg SHO: locate before the short; marking tickets short; close-out of fails; threshold securities; Rule 201 alternative uptick rule
Stock loan: lender, agent lender, borrower; cash collateral and the rebate; borrow fees; hard-to-borrow; recalls; buy-ins
Manufactured dividends and why they are not qualified dividends
Unlimited theoretical loss; short squeezes; margin on shorts (Reg T 150%)
Customer protection (Rule 15c3-3) and rehypothecation (140% of debit)
memorize: locate required before short sale
Rule 201: triggered by a 10% drop from prior close; applies rest of day and next day
short-sale fails closed out by start of trading on S+1
margin short: Reg T 150% (50% deposit)
rehypothecation limit 140% of debit balance
manufactured dividends taxed as ordinary income
traps: Short sellers PAY the dividend (to the lender)
Naked shorting = selling without borrowing/locating
Short sale risk is unlimited; long stock risk is limited to the investment
Buy-in: the lender recalls and the borrower can't return -> forced purchase
Protect a short with BUY CALL
calculations: Short P&L = (sale price - cover price) x shares - borrow costs - manufactured dividends
Rebate = cash collateral x (rebate rate)
trader_connection: Short selling -> securities lending; borrow cost as a market signal; squeeze dynamics as a liquidity cascade
Collateral mechanics connect to repo: same economics, different asset

days.title: Margin: leverage, collateral and the margin call
understand: Cash account vs margin account; margin agreement (credit agreement, hypothecation agreement, optional loan consent)
Regulation T (Fed) initial 50%; FINRA $2,000 minimum; maintenance 25% long / 30% short
Long account: LMV - DR = EQ; short account: SMV + EQ = CR
SMA as a line of credit: created by excess equity, sticky, can be used to buy or withdraw
Restricted accounts (equity below Reg T but above maintenance) and the 50% retention rule for withdrawals
Margin calls: Reg T call vs maintenance call; what happens if unmet
Which accounts cannot use margin: IRAs/retirement, UGMA/UTMA; what cannot be bought on margin (new issues for 30 days, options <= 9 months)
Freeriding in a cash account and the 90-day freeze; pattern day traders ($25,000)
memorize: Reg T 50%
FINRA minimum equity $2,000
maintenance 25% long, 30% short
PDT minimum equity $25,000
Reg T payment within settlement + 2 business days
freeriding -> 90-day freeze
new issues cannot be bought on margin for 30 days
margin disclosure statement at opening and annually
traps: The DEBIT balance does not change when the market moves; equity does
Short credit balance does not change with price
IRAs can NOT have margin (but can have limited-risk options)
Reg T is a Federal Reserve rule, enforced by FINRA on BDs
Minimum maintenance long: LMV at which EQ = 25% -> LMV = DR / 0.75
calculations: LMV - DR = EQ; SMV + EQ = CR
Excess equity = EQ - Reg T requirement
Maintenance call price (long) = DR / 0.75; (short) = CR / 1.30
Buying power = SMA / 0.50 (i.e., 2 x SMA)
trader_connection: Margin -> collateral/leverage: prime brokerage margin, portfolio margin, haircuts and initial margin in futures are the same idea
Margin calls are how price risk becomes liquidity risk; understand the call before you ever size a position

days.title: Opening accounts: registrations, KYC and AML
understand: Account registrations: individual, JTWROS, TIC, TOD, UGMA/UTMA, trusts, corporate, partnership, retirement
Discretion (written authorization, principal approval) vs time-and-price discretion; POA limited vs full; durable POA
Death and incapacity: what happens to each registration; POA ends at death
Account-opening information (Rule 4512), trusted contact person, Rule 2165 temporary holds for specified adults
Suitability (Rule 2111: reasonable-basis, customer-specific, quantitative) and Reg BI for retail recommendations; Form CRS
CIP (name, DOB, address, ID number), KYC (Rule 2090), AML program (Rule 3310), SARs, CTRs, OFAC, structuring
memorize: CIP 4 items: name, DOB, address, ID number
CTR: cash over $10,000 in a business day
SAR (BD): $5,000+ suspicious, within 30 days of detection; no tipping off
OFAC SDN list; block and report
trusted contact person must be 18+
time-and-price discretion valid only for the day granted
UGMA/UTMA: one custodian, one minor, no margin, irrevocable gifts
JTWROS -> to survivor; TIC -> to estate
traps: Structuring below $10,000 is itself a crime
Discretion requires WRITTEN authorization before the first discretionary trade
Time and price alone is not discretion
A POA (even durable) terminates at death
A trusted contact person has no authority to trade
Reg BI applies to recommendations to RETAIL customers
calculations: TIC ownership split at death
trader_connection: KYC/AML -> onboarding at every prime broker and ISDA counterparty; sanctions screening before any trade
Account structure determines who can pledge collateral and sign ISDAs

days.title: Retirement, education accounts and investment taxation
understand: Traditional IRA (pre-tax if deductible, taxed on withdrawal) vs Roth IRA (after-tax in, tax-free qualified out); earned income requirement
Qualified plans: 401(k), 403(b), 457 (no 10% penalty after separation), SEP, ERISA coverage
Rollovers (60 days, one indirect IRA-to-IRA per 12 months, 20% withholding from plans) vs trustee-to-trustee transfers
RMDs, 10% early-withdrawal penalty and exceptions, Roth 5-year rule
529 plans vs Coverdell ESAs; ABLE accounts; 529 plans as municipal fund securities
Capital gains (holding > 1 year), losses ($3,000 ordinary offset, carryforward), wash sales (30 days before/after), cost basis, gifts and inheritances (step-up)
Qualified vs ordinary dividends; return of capital
memorize: early withdrawal penalty 10% before 59 1/2
RMD age 73 (75 for those born 1960+)
60-day rollover; once per 12 months IRA-to-IRA
Coverdell $2,000/yr, contributions until 18, use by 30
529 K-12 tuition up to $20,000/yr (from 2026)
gift tax annual exclusion $19,000 (2026)
wash sale window 30 days before and after
net capital loss vs ordinary income $3,000/yr
traps: Roth contributions can be withdrawn anytime tax- and penalty-free; EARNINGS need 59 1/2 + 5 years
457 plans have no 10% early penalty on separation
Inherited securities get a step-up and are always long-term
Gifted securities carry the donor's basis
Wash sale DEFERS the loss (added to new basis) — it does not erase it
Contribution deadline is the tax filing deadline, not December 31
calculations: Holding-period start (day after trade date)
Wash sale basis adjustment
Capital gain/loss netting
After-tax return comparisons
trader_connection: Taxation -> after-tax P&L drives hedging choices (collars vs sales, harvesting losses without wash sales)
Tax lots and FIFO/specific ID matter in every trading P&L reconciliation
also_cover: IRA early-withdrawal exceptions (disability, death, SEPP, first home, education, medical): income tax still due, penalty waived
Dividend tax timing: taxable when paid; fund/REIT dividends declared Oct-Dec and paid in January count as received Dec 31

days.title: The rules of conduct: registration, communications and what gets you barred
understand: U4 (firm files at association; fingerprints; amend within 30 days) and U5 (within 30 days of termination)
SIE validity (4 years), qualification expiry (2 years after termination), Maintaining Qualifications Program (up to 5 years)
Continuing education: annual Regulatory Element, Firm Element
Statutory disqualification and reportable events
Communications: retail (principal pre-approval), correspondence (post-review), institutional; no promissory or misleading statements; retention
Insider trading (MNPI, tipper/tippee, ITSFEA penalties), manipulation, front running, marking the close, spoofing
Customer abuses: churning, unauthorized trading, sharing in accounts, guarantees, borrowing/lending, interpositioning, freeriding
OBAs (Rule 3270) and PSTs (Rule 3280); gifts (Rule 3220) and non-cash compensation
memorize: U4 amendments within 30 days
U5 within 30 days of termination
SIE valid 4 years
qualification lapses 2 years after termination (MQP up to 5)
Regulatory Element annually by Dec 31
gift limit $300 per person per year (effective 2026-03-30; was $100)
retail communication = more than 25 retail investors in 30 days
correspondence = 25 or fewer retail investors in 30 days
ITSFEA civil penalty up to 3x profit gained or loss avoided
records: blotters/ledgers 6 years; most other records 3 years
do-not-call: 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. local time of the called party
traps: Sharing in a customer account requires firm approval AND proportional sharing (except immediate family)
Guaranteeing a customer against loss is prohibited outright
PST for compensation must be approved AND supervised by the firm
OBA requires prior written NOTICE, not approval
The tipper can be liable even without trading
Correspondence does not need pre-approval; retail communications do
calculations: ITSFEA penalty computation
trader_connection: Front running and information barriers -> why trading desks are walled off from banking and research
Market manipulation rules shape how algos may post and cancel orders (spoofing)
also_cover: Records retention ladder: 3 years (U4/U5/fingerprints after termination, confirmations, statements, communications, trial balances), 4 (FINRA complaints), 5 (CTR, SAR, CIP after closing), 6 (blotters, account records after closing, MSRB complaints), lifetime (articles, partnership agreements, minute books, stock certificate books)
FINRA retains jurisdiction over a former registered person for 2 years after termination
Performance guarantees and personal buy-back promises are prohibited
